lead: A silicone chin implant is a solid, shaped alloplastic implant placed in front of the chin bone to increase projection. By moving the front of the chin forward it can improve the balance between chin, nose and lips and sharpen the profile and jawline. A general reference describes silicone as among the most commonly used chin implant materials: soft and flexible, but not bonding to tissue, so the pocket must be made precisely, with risks of movement, buckling or bone resorption; it can be removed easily.[1]

In looksmaxxing it is classed as a hardmaxx option and is often compared with porous polyethylene (Medpor), ePTFE and bone-cutting sliding genioplasty.[1] Chin augmentation is often done alongside rhinoplasty, and bone-based methods usually give a more dramatic change than implants.[1] Published material consists of case reports, surgeon series, reviews and a systematic review of complications across implant materials.[2][3][4][5]

chain: Silicone implant placed over the chin bone through an incision
Better-balanced profile and a more defined lower face
angle.text: The implant adds forward projection to a recessed chin, which changes the side profile and the proportions of the lower third of the face. It is placed in a pocket in front of the bone and can be removed if desired.

infobox: Does not bond to tissue; removable[1]
Plastic, ENT or oral and maxillofacial surgeons[1]

paras: Silicone implants come in many shapes and sizes, are available off the shelf and avoid a donor site, and artificial implants are described as biocompatible and FDA-cleared in general reference sources.[1] Implants are placed through an incision either under the chin (submental) or inside the lower lip (intraoral), and a pocket is created for the implant.[1] Because the material does not integrate with tissue, accurate pocket creation is stressed, and the implant can shift or buckle.[1]
After surgery patients are advised to minimise chewing and stay on soft foods for a period.[1]

sections.h: Comparison with other materials and methods
paras: Polyethylene (Medpor) is hard, porous and slightly flexible, with tissue growing into it, which holds it in place but makes removal much harder. ePTFE (Gore-Tex) is flexible and strong and is often screwed to bone, with tissue growth through its pores providing most of the fixation.[1] Silicone's smooth surface makes it easy to remove, while its main drawbacks are movement and resorption of bone where it contacts the jaw.[1]

Sliding genioplasty cuts a horseshoe-shaped segment from the lower jaw and moves it forward or backward, fixing it with a titanium plate and screws.[1] A 2018 French literature review reported that prosthetic genioplasty remained more frequently the source of serious complications such as infections, extrusions and bone erosions, had more limited indications than osseous genioplasty, and that osseous genioplasty offered better longevity.[3] A review on facial cosmetic surgery controversies discusses the benefits, disadvantages and considerations of osseous genioplasty versus alloplastic implants.[6] A 2023 systematic review in Annals of Plastic Surgery noted that silicone was historically the most commonly used implant while porous materials have grown in favour for improved fibrovascularization and stability, and compared complication rates (malposition, infection, extrusion, revision, removal, paresthesias and asymmetry) across 39 studies and more than 3,100 patients.[2]

Common and usually minor effects include swelling, haematoma and temporary weakness or numbness of the lower lip; less common are infection, bony changes, implant displacement and nerve damage, and surgeon experience is described as reducing risk.[1] Alloplastic chin implants can be associated with infection, bone resorption and secondary soft tissue deformities, which typically appear early after surgery but may occur later.[7] A case report describes an infected silicone chin implant in a 67-year-old woman who had received it 25 years earlier, after nearby dental implant surgery with non-ideal positioning led to contact with the silicone implant and absence of osseointegration.[8] A separate paper describes revision of an infected alloplastic chin implant by immediate osseous genioplasty with wire fixation.[7]

A 2025 single-surgeon series on facial feminization and masculinization surgery reports malar, chin and mandibular angle augmentation using fat grafting, stock silicone implants and custom implants.[9] Wikipedia notes that chin augmentation is sometimes pursued to improve confidence and self-esteem.[1] A 2024 review describes a custom chin implant made from piled-up ePTFE sheets, illustrating ongoing development of alternatives.[10]

The material reviewed consists of a systematic review of retrospective series, literature reviews, case reports and a retrospective single-surgeon series rather than randomised trials: a systematic review of alloplastic complications,[2] a review comparing prosthetic and osseous genioplasty,[3] an infected-implant revision,[7] an infected-implant case after dental implant surgery,[8] and a retrospective review of facial augmentation in transgender patients.[9] No randomised comparison of silicone with other chin implants was found.

name: Silicone chin implant

card.summary: Soft, removable synthetic implant for chin projection; common option, with published evidence mostly on complications.
card.note: Can shift, buckle, resorb bone or become infected, sometimes years later.

quick.overview:
A silicone chin implant is a shaped piece of silicone placed over the chin bone to add projection. It is among the most common chin implant materials and is relatively easy to remove.

In looksmaxxing it is one of the standard hardmaxx chin options, discussed alongside Medpor and sliding genioplasty.
quick.mechanism: The implant sits in a pocket and does not bond to tissue, so its position depends on the pocket being accurately made [1].
quick.risks: Reported issues include movement, buckling, bone resorption, infection (including late infection) and soft tissue deformity [1][2][3].
